L615: In (cite17†Ganyushkin and Mazorchuk, 2011 , Theorem 1(viii)), it is shown that, in this case, $\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta}$ is isomorphic to the Catalan monoid $\mathcal{C}_{n+1}$. The Catalan monoid $\mathcal{C}_{n+1}$ is the monoid of all order-preserving and order-decreasing total transformations of the set $[n+1]$. That is, the set of all $f:[n+1]\to[n+1]$ such that:
L616: 
L617:   1. (i)
L618: 
L619: $f(i)\leq f(j)$ for $i,j\in[n+1]$ with $i\leq j$ (order-preserving);
L620: 
L621:   2. (ii)
L622: 
L623: $f(i)\leq i$ for $i\in[n+1]$ (order-decreasing).
L624: The operation in $\mathcal{C}_{n+1}$ is the usual composition and the unit element is the identity on $[n+1]$. For $f,g\in\mathcal{C}_{n+1}$, we denote by $fg=f\circ g$.
L625: 
L626: Catalan monoids and their presentations were studied in cite57†Solomon (1996) . In (cite58†Stanley, 1999 , 6.25(g)), it was shown that $|\mathcal{C}_{n+1}|=C_{n+1}$, where $C_{n}=\frac{1}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}$ denotes the $n$-th Catalan number.
L627: In the proof of (cite17†Ganyushkin and Mazorchuk, 2011 , Theorem 1(vii)), the authors use the fact that the transformations $T_{i}$ for $i=1,2,\dots,n$, defined by
L628: 
L629:  | $$T_{i}(j)=\begin{cases}i,&j=i+1,\\
L630: j,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}$$  |
L631: 
L632: generate $\mathcal{C}_{n+1}$. The corresponding isomorphism of monoids from $\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta}$ to $\mathcal{C}_{n+1}$ is then given by the unique extension of the mapping $x_{i}\mapsto T_{i}$ and we denote it by $\tau$.
L633: ### Step 1: Determine $A_{\Theta}$ and idempotents
L634: 
L635: Since $\Theta$ is acyclic, we have $A_{\Theta}=\mathbbm{2}^{[n]}$. For nonempty $X=\{i_{1},i_{2},\dots,i_{k}\}\subseteq[n]$ with $i_{1}>i_{2}>\dots>i_{k}$, we have that $i_{j}\to i_{j^{\prime}}$ implies $j>j^{\prime}$. By Lemma cite38†2.7 , we have
L636: 
L637:  | $$e_{X}=x_{i_{k}}\dots x_{i_{2}}x_{i_{1}}.$$  |  | (4)
L638: Hence, in this case, idempotents are written as products in which the indices of the generators increase from left to right. Observe that in the Kiselman monoid, we have the converse case. We also denote $T_{X}=\tau(e_{X})$. In particular, $T_{\emptyset}$ is the identity on $[n+1]$.
L639: Since $\tau$ is an isomorphism of monoids, $e_{X}e_{Y}$ is an idempotent in $\mathrm{HK}_{\Theta}$ if and only if $T_{X}T_{Y}$ is an idempotent in $\mathcal{C}_{n+1}$ and $e_{X}e_{Y}=e_{X\cup Y}$ if and only if $T_{X}T_{Y}=T_{X\cup Y}$. By (cite49†3 ), we then have
L640: 
L641:  | $$p(X,Y)\iff e_{X}e_{Y}\text{ is an idempotent}\iff T_{X}T_{Y}\text{ is an idempotent}\iff T_{X}T_{Y}=T_{X\cup Y}.$$  |  | (5)
L642: ### Step 2: Determine the predicate $p$
L643: 
L644: For $X\subseteq[n]$, define the following set
L645: 
L646:  | $$F_{X}=[n+1]\setminus\{x+1\mid x\in X\}.$$  |
L647: 
L648: Note that $1\in F_{X}$ for any $X\subseteq[n]$. For $a\in[n+1]$, we have
L649: 
L650:  | $$a\in F_{X}\iff a-1\notin X.$$  |  | (6)
L651: 
L652: For any $X,Y\subseteq[n]$, we also have
L653: 
L654:  | $$F_{X\cup Y}=F_{X}\cap F_{Y}.$$  |  | (7)
L655: 
L656: ###### Proposition 4.1.
L657: 
L658: Let $X\subseteq[n]$. Then we have
L659: 
L660:  | $$T_{X}(t)=\max(F_{X}\cap[t]),$$  |
L661: 
L662: for all $t\in[n+1]$.
L663: ###### Proof.
L664: 
L665: We prove the formula by induction on $|X|$. If $X=\emptyset$, then we have $F_{X}=[n+1]$. Hence $F_{X}\cap[t]=[t]$ for all $t\in[n+1]$. Since $T_{X}$ is the identity on $[n+1]$, we indeed have
L666: 
L667:  | $$T_{X}(t)=t=\max([t])=\max(F_{X}\cap[t]).$$  |
L668: 
L669: Let $|X|=r$ with $0<r\leq n$ and assume that the formula in the statement holds for all sets $Y\subseteq[n]$ with $|Y|<r$. Write $X$ as
L670: 
L671:  | $$X=\{i_{1},i_{2},\dots,i_{r-1},i_{r}\}$$  |
L672: with $i_{1}<i_{2}<\dots<i_{r-1}<i_{r}$. Denote by $Y=X\setminus\{i_{r}\}$. Then $|Y|=r-1$ and by the induction hypothesis, we have
L673: 
L674:  | $$T_{Y}(t)=\max(F_{Y}\cap[t]).$$  |
L675: 
L676: By the definition of $T_{X}$ and (cite59†4 ), we have $T_{X}=T_{Y}T_{i_{r}}$. Hence
L677: 
L678:  | $$T_{X}(t)=(T_{Y}\circ T_{i_{r}})(t)=T_{Y}(T_{i_{r}}(t))=\max(F_{Y}\cap[T_{i_{r}}(t)]).$$  |
L679: 
L680: Observe that
L681: 
L682:  | $$F_{X}=F_{Y\cup\{i_{r}\}}=F_{Y}\cap F_{\{i_{r}\}}=F_{Y}\setminus\{i_{r}+1\}.$$  |
L683: Now we consider different cases on the value of $t\in[n+1]$.
L684: 
L685: Case 1: $t<i_{r}+1$. In this case, we have $T_{i_{r}}(t)=t$. We also have
L686: 
L687:  | $$[t]=[t]\setminus\{i_{r}+1\}.$$  |
L688: 
L689: Hence
L690: 
L691:  | $$F_{Y}\cap[T_{i_{r}}(t)]=F_{Y}\cap[t]=F_{Y}\cap([t]\setminus\{i_{r}+1\})=(F_{Y}\setminus\{i_{r}+1\})\cap[t]=F_{X}\cap[t].$$  |
L692: 
L693: Thus,
L694: 
L695:  | $$T_{X}(t)=\max(F_{Y}\cap[T_{i_{r}}(t)])=\max(F_{X}\cap[t]).$$  |
L696: 
L697: Case 2: $t=i_{r}+1$. In this case, we have $T_{i_{r}}(t)=i_{r}$ and also
L698:  | $$[i_{r}]=[i_{r}]\setminus\{i_{r}+1\}.$$  |
L699: 
L700: Hence
L701: 
L702:  | $$F_{Y}\cap[T_{i_{r}}(t)]=F_{Y}\cap[i_{r}]=F_{Y}\cap([i_{r}]\setminus\{i_{r}+1\})=(F_{Y}\setminus\{i_{r}+1\})\cap[i_{r}]=F_{X}\cap[i_{r}].$$  |
L703: 
L704: Since $i_{r}+1\notin F_{X}$, we have
L705: 
L706:  | $$F_{X}\cap[i_{r}+1]=F_{X}\cap([i_{r}]\cup\{i_{r}+1\})=(F_{X}\cap[i_{r}])\cup(F_{X}\cap\{i_{r}+1\})=(F_{X}\cap[i_{r}])\cup\emptyset=F_{X}\cap[i_{r}].$$  |
L707: 
L708: Thus we obtain
L709: 
L710:  | $$F_{Y}\cap[T_{i_{r}}(t)]=F_{X}\cap[i_{r}]=F_{X}\cap[i_{r}+1]=F_{X}\cap[t].$$  |
L711: Therefore, we again conclude
L712: 
L713:  | $$T_{X}(t)=\max(F_{Y}\cap[T_{i_{r}}(t)])=\max(F_{X}\cap[t]).$$  |
L714: 
L715: Case 3: $t>i_{r}+1$. Since $i_{1}<i_{2}<\dots<i_{r}<i_{r}+1<t$, we obtain $i_{j}+1<t$ for every $j=1,2,\dots,r$. Hence $T_{i_{j}}(t)=t$ for all $j=1,2,\dots,r$. Thus,
L716: 
L717:  | $$T_{X}(t)=(T_{i_{1}}T_{i_{2}}\dots T_{i_{r}})(t)=t,$$  |
L718: 
L719: since each $T_{i_{j}}$ fixes $t$. On the other hand, since $t-1>i_{r}=\max X$, we have $t-1\notin X$, and hence (cite60†6 ) implies $t\in F_{X}$. It follows that
L720:  | $$\max(F_{X}\cap[t])=t,$$  |
L721: 
L722: which implies
L723: 
L724:  | $$T_{X}(t)=t=\max(F_{X}\cap[t]).$$  |
L725: 
L726: Hence, for all $t\in[n+1]$, we have
L727: 
L728:  | $$T_{X}(t)=\max(F_{X}\cap[t]).$$  |
L729: 
L730: This concludes the induction step and hence the proof is finished. ∎
L731: 
L732: For $f:[n+1]\to[n+1]$, denote by
L733: 
L734:  | $$\mathrm{Im}(f)=\{f(i)\mid i\in[n+1]\}\quad\text{and}\quad\mathrm{Fix}(f)=\{i\in[n+1]\mid f(i)=i\},$$  |
L735: 
L736: the range of $f$ and the set of fixed points of $f$.

L269: ###### Definition 3.1.
L270: 
L271: For $X,Y\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}$, define the predicate $p_{\Theta}$ as follows. Condition $p_{\Theta}(X,Y)$ holds if and only if there do not exist $x_{b}\in Y\setminus X$, $x_{a}\in X\setminus Y$, $r\in\mathbb{N}_{0}$, and $x_{i_{1}},\dots,x_{i_{r}}\in X\cap Y$ such that
L272: 
L273:  | $$x_{b}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{i_{1}}\overset{\Theta}{\to}\dots\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{i_{r}}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{a}.$$  |
L274: ###### Remark 3.2.
L275: 
L276: If $r=0$, a chain $x_{b}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{i_{1}}\overset{\Theta}{\to}\dots\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{i_{r}}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{a}$ is interpreted as $x_{b}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{a}$.
L277: 
L278: ###### Lemma 3.3.
L279: 
L280: Let $X,Y\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}$. Then $p_{\Theta}(X,Y)$ holds if and only if there does not exist a directed path in $\Theta[X\cup Y]$ whose startpoint lies in $Y\setminus X$ and whose endpoint lies in $X\setminus Y$.
L281: ###### Proof.
L282: 
L283: If there is no directed path in $\Theta[X\cup Y]$ which starts in some vertex of $Y\setminus X$ and ends in some vertex of $X\setminus Y$, then $p_{\Theta}(X,Y)$ must hold. Assume $p_{\Theta}(X,Y)$ holds. Suppose there exists a directed path
L284: 
L285:  | $$x_{i_{1}}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{i_{2}}\overset{\Theta}{\to}\dots\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{i_{k}},$$  |
L286: 
L287: such that $x_{i_{1}}\in Y\setminus X$, $x_{i_{k}}\in X\setminus Y$, and $x_{i_{1}},x_{i_{2}},\dots,x_{i_{k}}\in X\cup Y$. Let
L288:  | $$j_{1}=\max\{j\in\{1,\dots,k\}\mid x_{i_{j}}\in Y\setminus X\}\quad\text{and}\quad j_{2}=\min\{j\in\{j_{1}+1,\dots,k\}\mid x_{i_{j}}\in X\setminus Y\}.$$  |
L289: 
L290: Since $x_{i_{k}}\in X\setminus Y$ and $j_{1}<k$, the index $j_{2}$ is well-defined, and $j_{1}<j_{2}$. Then the directed path
L291: 
L292:  | $$x_{i_{j_{1}}}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{i_{j_{1}+1}}\overset{\Theta}{\to}\dots\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{i_{j_{2}-1}}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{i_{j_{2}}}$$  |
L293: starts in $Y\setminus X$ and ends in $X\setminus Y$. Moreover, the vertices $x_{i_{j_{1}+1}},\dots,x_{i_{j_{2}-1}}$ lie in $X\cap Y$; by the maximality of $j_{1}$, none of them lies in $Y\setminus X$, and by the minimality of $j_{2}$, none of them lies in $X\setminus Y$. Since all vertices of the directed path lie in $X\cup Y$, the vertices $x_{i_{j_{1}+1}},\dots,x_{i_{j_{2}-1}}$ must lie in $X\cap Y$. This contradicts the fact that $p_{\Theta}(X,Y)$ holds and concludes the proof. ∎
L294: Let $w=x_{i_{1}}x_{i_{2}}\dots x_{i_{k}}\in F(V_{\Theta})$ be a word, where $x_{i_{1}},x_{i_{2}},\dots,x_{i_{k}}\in F(V_{\Theta})$ are letters. A word of the form $u=x_{i_{j_{1}}}x_{i_{j_{2}}}\dots x_{i_{j_{l}}}$ with $1\leq j_{1}<j_{2}<\dots<j_{l}\leq k$ is called a quasi-subword of $w$. Moreover, the empty word is a quasi-subword of any word. From the definition of $\to$, it follows that if $u\overset{*}{\to}v$, then $v$ is a quasi-subword of $u$.
L295: ###### Proposition 3.4.
L296: 
L297: Let $X,Y\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}$. If $e_{X}e_{Y}$ is an idempotent in $\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}$, then $p_{\Theta}(X,Y)$ holds.
L298: ###### Proof.
L299: 
L300: Assume $p_{\Theta}(X,Y)$ does not hold. We show that $e_{X}e_{Y}$ is not an idempotent. Suppose that, on the contrary, $e_{X}e_{Y}$ is an idempotent. We now construct a contradiction. Let $w_{X}$ be a normal form of $e_{X}$ and let $w_{Y}$ be a normal form of $e_{Y}$. Lemma cite43†2.12 implies that $w_{X}$ is $X$-topological and $w_{Y}$ is $Y$-topological. We also have $\pi(w_{X}w_{Y})=e_{X}e_{Y}$. Since $e_{X}e_{Y}$ is an idempotent, by Proposition cite44†2.8 , we have
L301:  | $$X\cup Y\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}\quad\text{and}\quad e_{X}e_{Y}=e_{X\cup Y}.$$  |
L302: 
L303: Let $u\in F(V_{\Theta})$ be a normal form of $e_{X\cup Y}$ with $w_{X}w_{Y}\overset{*}{\to}u$. Such a word $u$ exists by Theorem cite41†2.4 (cite45†ii ) and $\pi(w_{X}w_{Y})=e_{X}e_{Y}=e_{X\cup Y}$. By Lemma cite43†2.12 , $u$ is $X\cup Y$-topological.
L304: 
L305: Since $p_{\Theta}(X,Y)$ does not hold, there exist $x_{b}\in Y\setminus X$, $x_{a}\in X\setminus Y$, $r\in\mathbb{N}_{0}$, and $x_{i_{1}},\dots,x_{i_{r}}\in X\cap Y$ such that
L306:  | $$x_{b}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{i_{1}}\overset{\Theta}{\to}\dots\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{i_{r}}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{a}.$$  |
L307: Observe that each of the letters $x_{a}$ and $x_{b}$ occurs exactly once in $w_{X}w_{Y}$, and hence they occur exactly once in $u$, since an elementary cancellation cannot delete a letter that occurs only once. Moreover, $x_{a}$ occurs to the left of $x_{b}$ in $w_{X}w_{Y}$, since $x_{a}$ occurs in $w_{X}$ and $x_{b}$ occurs in $w_{Y}$. Since $w_{X}w_{Y}\overset{*}{\to}u$, $u$ is a quasi-subword of $w_{X}w_{Y}$, and hence $x_{a}$ occurs to the left of $x_{b}$ in $u$ as well.
L308: If $r=0$, then $x_{b}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{a}$. Hence $x_{a}$ must occur to the right of $x_{b}$ in $u$, since there are no arrows from right to left in $u$, as $u$ is $X\cup Y$-topological. This contradicts the last conclusion of the previous paragraph, which established that $x_{a}$ occurs to the left of $x_{b}$ in $u$. Now assume $r>0$.
L309: Since $u$ is $X\cup Y$-topological and $x_{i_{1}},\dots,x_{i_{r}}\in X\cap Y\subseteq X\cup Y$, each of the letters $x_{i_{1}},\dots,x_{i_{r}}$ occurs exactly once in $u$. Since $x_{b}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{i_{1}}$ and $u$ has no arrows from right to left, $x_{i_{1}}$ occurs to the right of $x_{b}$ in $u$. It follows that for $1<t\leq r$, $x_{i_{t}}$ occurs to the right of $x_{i_{t-1}}$ in $u$, since $x_{i_{t-1}}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{i_{t}}$ and $u$ has no arrows from right to left.
L310: Inductively, we conclude that each $x_{i_{t}}$ for $1\leq t\leq r$ occurs to the right of $x_{b}$ in $u$. Finally, it follows from $x_{i_{r}}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{a}$ and the fact that $u$ has no arrows from right to left that $x_{a}$ occurs to the right of $x_{i_{r}}$ in $u$, and hence $x_{a}$ occurs to the right of $x_{b}$ in $u$. In the previous paragraph, however, it is established that $x_{a}$ occurs to the left of $x_{b}$ in $u$. Hence we have reached a contradiction, and the proof is complete. ∎
L311: ###### Proposition 3.5.
L312: 
L313: Let $X,Y\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}$. If $p_{\Theta}(X,Y)$ holds, then $e_{X}e_{Y}$ is an idempotent in $\mathbf{HK}_{\Theta}$.
L314: ###### Proof.
L315: 
L316: Assume $p_{\Theta}(X,Y)$ holds. To prove that $e_{X}e_{Y}$ is an idempotent, by Proposition cite44†2.8 , we need to show $X\cup Y\in\mathcal{A}_{\Theta}$ and $e_{X}e_{Y}=e_{X\cup Y}$.
L317: 
L318: Denote $I=X\cap Y$ and
L319: 
L320:  | $$R=\{x_{i}\in I\mid\exists x_{b}\in Y\setminus X,r\in\mathbb{N}_{0},x_{i_{1}},\dots,x_{i_{r}}\in I:x_{b}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{i_{1}}\overset{\Theta}{\to}\dots\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{i_{r}}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{i}\}.$$  |
L321: 
L322: Also set $S=I\setminus R$. We denote by
L323:  | $$M=(Y\setminus X)\cup R\quad\text{and}\quad N=(X\setminus Y)\cup S.$$  |  | (1)
L324: 
L325: Observe that since $R,S\subseteq I=X\cap Y$, the above unions are disjoint. Then we further have
L326: 
L327:  | $$X=N\cup R,\quad Y=M\cup S,\quad X\cup Y=N\cup M.$$  |  | (2)
L328: 
L329: The unions on the right-hand sides of these equalities are disjoint as well. The key observation is the following claim.
L330: ###### Claim.
L331: 
L332: There are no arrows starting in $M$ and ending in $N$.
L333: ###### Proof of the claim.
L334: We argue by contradiction. Let $x_{i}\in M$, $x_{j}\in N$ and suppose $x_{i}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{j}$. Now we consider cases on $x_{i}$ and $x_{j}$ based on (cite46†1 ). Since $p_{\Theta}(X,Y)$ holds, we cannot have $x_{i}\in Y\setminus X$ and $x_{j}\in X\setminus Y$. If $x_{i}\in Y\setminus X$ and $x_{j}\in S$, this implies $x_{j}\in R$ by the definition of $R$, which is a contradiction since $R\cap S=\emptyset$.
L335: If $x_{i}\in R$ and $x_{j}\in X\setminus Y$, then by the definition of $R$, there exist $x_{b}\in Y\setminus X$, $r\in\mathbb{N}_{0}$, and $x_{i_{1}},\dots,x_{i_{r}}\in I$ such that
L336:  | $$x_{b}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{i_{1}}\overset{\Theta}{\to}\dots\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{i_{r}}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{i}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{j}.$$  |
L337: 
L338: Since $x_{i}\in R\subseteq I$ and $x_{j}\in X\setminus Y$, this contradicts the fact that $p_{\Theta}(X,Y)$ holds. If $x_{i}\in R$ and $x_{j}\in S$, we have some $x_{b}\in Y\setminus X$, $r\in\mathbb{N}_{0}$, and $x_{i_{1}},\dots,x_{i_{r}}\in I$ such that
L339:  | $$x_{b}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{i_{1}}\overset{\Theta}{\to}\dots\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{i_{r}}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{i}\overset{\Theta}{\to}x_{j}.$$  |
L340:
